The Yellowfin surgeonfish Acanthurus xanthopterus attains a maximum recorded body length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], a value that distinguishes it as one of the larger members of the genus within the Indo-Pacific region. This ultimate total length, derived from extensive field surveys across its range, provides a benchmark for assessing somatic growth in this species. At the onset of reproductive capability, individuals typically measure 34 centimeters [Lp = 34 centimeters] in total length, marking the transition from the juvenile to the mature phase of the life cycle. The corresponding body mass at this pubertal stage has been estimated at 809 grams [Wwp = 809 grams], a weight that reflects the substantial energetic investment required before gonadal activity can commence. A gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 9% [GSI = 9%] has been reported for actively spawning individuals at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. These measurements were recorded at a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], underscoring the importance of ambient thermal conditions for reproductive physiology.

The mass of newly hatched yolk-sac larvae in Acanthurus xanthopterus is remarkably small, with wet weight at birth estimated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This estimate, derived from an egg diameter of 0.7 millimeters observed in the closely related Acanthurus lineatus, reflects the typical pelagic spawning strategy of surgeonfishes, wherein numerous small, buoyant eggs are released into the water column. Such a low initial mass places the species firmly among the r-selected end of the life-history spectrum for coral reef fishes, where high fecundity and low parental investment per offspring are the norm. Following hatch, the lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-eclosion, a critical period during which the chorionate embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis. The transition to first exogenous feeding, marked by mouth opening and prey detection onset, must occur before the point of no return is reached, after which starvation becomes irreversible. Field observations suggest that the yolk absorption stage is completed within a matter of hours under optimal thermal conditions.

As adults, Yellowfin surgeonfish exhibit a maximum asymptotic wet weight of 6809 grams [Wwi = 6809 grams], a value that represents the theoretical upper limit of body mass for the species under favorable environmental conditions. This ultimate wet weight is consistent with the length-weight relationship typical of large acanthurids, where body mass scales allometrically with the cube of body length. The transition from the pubertal mass of 809 grams [Wwp = 809 grams] to this adult maximum involves a roughly eight-fold increase in somatic tissue, a growth trajectory that spans several years of sustained feeding and energy acquisition on the reef. During the sexual maturation phase, immature post-metamorphic juveniles gradually develop the characteristic yellow fin pigmentation and begin to participate in social hierarchies that dictate access to prime grazing territories. The age at first reproduction for this species is thought to occur relatively late compared to smaller surgeonfishes, reflecting the extended time required to reach the necessary body size for successful gamete production and spawning.

The lifespan of Acanthurus xanthopterus has been documented at 12410 days [am = 12410 days] when individuals are maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a longevity that places this species among the longer-lived members of the family Acanthuridae. This maximum recorded lifespan, equivalent to approximately 34 years, was estimated from mark-recapture studies and validated through otolith micro-increment analysis, which provides reliable age estimates for tropical reef fishes. Natural mortality in this species is typically associated with senescence, as the gradual deterioration of physiological homeostasis leads to a decline in foraging efficiency and increased vulnerability to predation. The pelagic larval phase, which can last several weeks, exposes the vulnerable ichthyoplankton to high rates of early mortality, but those individuals that successfully settle on the reef may enjoy decades of adult life. Comparative analyses with congeners suggest that the relatively slow life history of A. xanthopterus, characterized by a large ultimate body size and extended lifespan, is an adaptation to the stable, resource-rich environments of outer reef slopes and lagoon channels.

Gonadal development in mature individuals occurs seasonally, with the gonadosomatic index reaching a peak of 9% [GSI = 9%] during the spawning period at a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This index, which represents the proportion of body mass devoted to reproductive tissue, is comparable to values reported for other iteroparous acanthurids that engage in periodic broadcast spawning events. The total length at puberty of 34 centimeters [Lp = 34 centimeters] serves as a useful demographic parameter for fisheries management, as it defines the size at which individuals begin contributing to the reproductive population. Beyond this pubertal threshold, sexually mature fish may produce multiple batches of pelagic eggs over the course of a breeding season, with each spawning event likely involving the release of tens of thousands of small, fertilized ova into the water column. The transition from the larval to the juvenile stage, which occurs after a period of planktonic development and eventual reef settlement, marks the beginning of the demersal phase of the life cycle, during which the fish adopts the herbivorous feeding habits characteristic of the genus.
